newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ govt's fiscal discipline unprecedented - Birch.
newsitem.headline: NZ govt's fiscal discipline unprecedented - Birch.

text.p: Finance Minister Bill Birch said on Tuesday the new government was committed to a level of fiscal discipline not seen before in New Zealand.

"Both National and New Zealand First have...committed themselves, in the Coalition Agreement, to a level of fiscal discipline that is, to my knowledge, without precedent in this country," he told a Wellington business breakfast meeting.
Birch said all the government's advice was that a blow-out in spending would seriously affect growth, exports and employment performance.
Recognising that, it had deferred for a year the tax cuts legislated in 1996.
Birch said policy directions, key projects and overall spending limits were clearly specified in the Coalition Agreement.

The agreement contained signed undertakings that additional spending, together with the abolition of the superannuation surcharge, would not exceed the December economic and fiscal update by more than NZ$1.2 billion in 1997-98, $1.7 billion in 1998-99 and $2.1 billion in 1999-2000.

Birch said the coalition government was aware that new initiatives could cost less in the first year than when fully implemented in subsequent years. It would carefully measure the full implication of Year One spending on the fiscal parameters in Year Three.

Birch said the additional money to be made available under the Coalition Agreement was reserved in the main part for new output. The government would not permit it simply to boost the pay of existing bureaucrats.
Resources were already available to meet a lot of additional pressures, if the NZ$33 billion the government was already spending on existing programmes was spent to the best possible advantage.

"We expect the public sector, just like the private sector, to produce ongoing gains in productivity every year, and like the private sector, to meet wage rises from these gains, or by reducing purchases of low-priority outputs," Birch said.
He said rigorous systematic processes were in place to achieve the government's fiscal objectives.
